core/landscape/database.py:R5:_safe_data: database.py:174 `values = value if isinstance(value, tuple) else (value,)`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance narrowing a declared library union. SQLAlchemy types `URL.query` as an immutable mapping of `str` to `str | tuple[str, ...]` — a single occurrence of a query parameter yields the bare string, a repeated occurrence (`?odbc_connect=a&odbc_connect=b`) yields a tuple of every value. This site is the WIDENING half of a widen/restore pair: it lifts both arms to a uniform tuple so the following line can run `_scrub_odbc_connect_value` over EVERY occurrence. That matters for credential safety specifically — `_safe_database_descriptor` exists to strip credentials out of a database URL before it is interpolated into a `SchemaCompatibilityError` message, and an ODBC connection string carries `PWD=` inside the parameter value. Treating a repeated `odbc_connect` as a single scalar would scrub only the first occurrence and leak the rest into an operator-visible error. The check is not masking a contract violation: both arms of SQLAlchemy's declared union are handled and there is no third arm to fall through. It is also not a Tier-3 parse — the connection string was already parsed by `make_url` at line 164 (whose failure is caught and returns the redacted placeholder), so what is being discriminated here is a SQLAlchemy-owned value with a SQLAlchemy-guaranteed type, which ADR-032 says to type nominally, not to re-parse. INVALIDATED IF: SQLAlchemy narrows `URL.query` values to a single type (the widen/restore pair then becomes dead and both sites should be deleted, not re-justified); or the scrubbing loop stops applying `_scrub_odbc_connect_value` to every element of `values`, at which point the widening no longer buys the multi-occurrence coverage that justifies it.

database.py:176 `safe_query[key] = scrubbed_values if isinstance(value, tuple) else scrubbed_values[0]`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance narrowing a declared library union. This is the RESTORE half of the widen/restore pair opened at line 174, and it tests the same `value` — deliberately the original, not the widened `values` — because its job is to put the scrubbed result back at the caller's original cardinality. `safe_query` is handed to `parsed.set(query=safe_query).render_as_string(hide_password=True)`, and SQLAlchemy renders a tuple-valued query parameter as repeated `key=` pairs but a string-valued one as a single pair. Dropping the distinction would silently rewrite the URL's shape in the diagnostic: a single-valued `odbc_connect` would render as a one-element repeat, and — worse in the other direction — a multi-valued one collapsed to `scrubbed_values[0]` would make an operator-facing error message claim the URL had fewer parameters than it did. The isinstance therefore preserves an observable property of the input rather than hiding a contract violation; the failure it prevents is a misleading diagnostic, not a crash. INVALIDATED IF: the widening at line 174 is removed or changed to preserve cardinality itself (this restore would then be reading a variable that no longer distinguishes the cases); or `safe_query` stops flowing into `URL.set(query=...)` and is instead consumed by something with no cardinality semantics, in which case the branch is pointless and should be deleted.
core/landscape/database.py:R5:_shared_co: database.py:210 `if not isinstance(engine.pool, StaticPool):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance on a library class used as a dispatch control. `engine.pool` is a SQLAlchemy `Pool`, and `StaticPool` is the one concrete implementation that shares a SINGLE DBAPI connection across every thread; every other pool SQLAlchemy ships (the production `QueuePool`, `NullPool`, `SingletonThreadPool`) hands out a connection per thread. The isinstance is a capability test on a concurrency contract, and the class identity IS the contract — there is no attribute or public flag on `Pool` that reports 'shares one connection', so a structural probe would have nothing honest to read. Returning `None` here is not a swallowed failure, it is the documented lock-free fast path: the block comment above the function records that file-backed production engines already get safety from QueuePool plus WAL/BEGIN IMMEDIATE/busy_timeout, and that making them take an app-level lock would regress the epoch-21 multi-writer design. The narrow direction of the test is what keeps it honest — an unrecognised future pool falls into the `None`/no-lock arm, which is correct for every per-thread-connection pool and only unsafe for another connection-sharing pool. INVALIDATED IF: production moves off `QueuePool` onto a connection-sharing pool, or SQLAlchemy adds a second `StaticPool`-like class; either makes the unrecognised-pool arm wrong and the test must become an explicit allow-list of per-thread pools that raises on anything unknown. Also invalidated if `StaticPool` stops being test-only in this codebase, since the whole rationale for a lock this narrow is that only `LandscapeDB.in_memory()` reaches it.
core/landscape/database.py:R5:_sqlite_ep: database.py:793 `if isinstance(bind, Connection):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance narrowing a union this codebase declares itself. The parameter is annotated `bind: Engine | Connection` — an ELSPETH-owned signature over two SQLAlchemy classes — and the branch exists because the two arms carry different RESOURCE OWNERSHIP contracts, not merely different types. A `Connection` was opened by the caller and is very likely inside an open transaction, so this function must execute `PRAGMA user_version` on it directly and must NOT close it; an `Engine` owns no live connection, so this function opens its own with `with bind.connect()` and closes it on exit. Collapsing the branches either leaks a connection per call or closes a caller's transaction out from under it. This is exactly the ADR-032 'nominally type what ELSPETH owns' case: the union is ours, both arms are enumerated, and neither is a defensive guess about malformed data. What this specific site reads is the SQLite schema epoch, and the surrounding function is fail-closed by construction — `scalar_one()` raises if the PRAGMA returns no row rather than defaulting the epoch, so a corrupt target cannot be silently treated as compatible. INVALIDATED IF: the signature narrows to a single type (the branch is then dead code and should be deleted rather than re-justified), or the Engine arm stops using a context manager, since 'the Engine arm cleans up after itself' is half of why the split is justified.

core/landscape/database.py:R5:LandscapeD: database.py:1228 `value = raw_value if isinstance(raw_value, str) else raw_value[0]`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance narrowing a declared library union. Third site over SQLAlchemy's `URL.query` union (`str | tuple[str, ...]`), but unlike the pair at 174/176 this one deliberately DISCARDS the multi-occurrence case by taking `raw_value[0]`, and that asymmetry is the justification. The values here are being forwarded into `sqlite3.connect()` keyword arguments and SQLite URI parameters, and every one of those is scalar by definition: `check_same_thread` and `uri` are coerced to bool, `timeout` to float, `detect_types` and `cached_statements` to int, and the leftovers become `uri_params` entries that are rendered into a single `file:` URI. There is no kwarg here that could accept a tuple, so a repeated query parameter has no meaningful representation and last-wins/first-wins is a genuine choice rather than a dropped error; taking `[0]` matches how SQLAlchemy's own pysqlite dialect extracts connect arguments on the unencrypted path, which the block comment above cites as the parity target. This is not a Tier-3 parse of untrusted input either — `make_url` has already parsed the URL and the SQLCipher-specific validation above (driver must be SQLite, database must be file-backed, not `:memory:`) has already raised on the shapes this function refuses. INVALIDATED IF: a genuinely list-valued SQLite connect parameter is added to `_CONNECT_KWARGS` (silently dropping its later values would then be a real defect and the site must handle the tuple arm); or the SQLCipher path stops mirroring the non-encrypted `create_engine` extraction, which is the parity argument that makes first-wins the right choice rather than an arbitrary one.
core/landscape/journal.py:R5:LandscapeJo: journal.py:726 `if isinstance(parameters, list):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance as structural dispatch in a recursive walk. `_normalize_parameters` renders the DBAPI parameter payload SQLAlchemy hands the journal's execution hook into a JSON-safe shape, because `_serialize_record` then calls `json.dumps(safe, allow_nan=False)` and any non-serializable member is a Tier-1 audit failure that raises `AuditIntegrityError`. The `list` arm is the executemany case: SQLAlchemy passes a SEQUENCE OF PARAMETER SETS, so this arm recurses per element and each element is itself a dict or tuple handled by the arms below. The concrete-type test is required rather than lazy: the obvious structural alternative — testing `Sequence` or probing for `__iter__` — is WRONG here because `str` and `bytes` are both sequences and are exactly the leaf values that must fall through to `serialize_datetime` intact; iterating a parameter string character by character would corrupt every audited SQL parameter. `isinstance` against the concrete builtin is the only test that separates a container from a string. Nothing is masked: the final `return serialize_datetime(parameters)` is a total fallback, so an unrecognised type is carried to `json.dumps`, which raises rather than silently dropping it. INVALIDATED IF: the total leaf fallback is replaced by something that swallows or defaults an unserializable value (the arms would then be hiding a Tier-1 violation instead of routing around one), or `_serialize_record` stops raising `AuditIntegrityError` on `TypeError`.

journal.py:728 `if isinstance(parameters, tuple):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance as structural dispatch in a recursive walk. Distinct arm from the `list` test above it, and the pair is not redundant: SQLAlchemy hands a `tuple` for a SINGLE positional parameter set under the qmark/format paramstyles that SQLite and most drivers use, while a `list` means the executemany sequence. Both arms recurse elementwise and both emit a JSON array, and that convergence is deliberate rather than duplication — JSON has no tuple, so normalising the positional set to a list is what makes the persisted `record['parameters']` type-uniform for every downstream reader, notably `_enrich_with_payloads`, which casts it to `list[object]` and indexes it. This arm is kept separate from the `list` arm rather than merged into one `isinstance(parameters, (list, tuple))` test because the two describe different SQLAlchemy payload shapes and a future change that must treat the executemany sequence differently from a positional set (for example, capping how many parameter sets are journalled) has to split them again; merging them would buy one fewer lint finding and nothing else. As at 726, a concrete-type test is mandatory because `str`/`bytes` must reach the leaf fallback rather than be walked. INVALIDATED IF: `record['parameters']` stops being consumed as a list (the tuple-to-list normalisation would then be unmotivated), or the leaf fallback stops being total.

journal.py:730 `if isinstance(parameters, dict):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance as structural dispatch in a recursive walk. This is the named-paramstyle arm — SQLAlchemy hands a mapping of bind-parameter name to value — and it is the only arm that recurses over VALUES while preserving KEYS, because those keys are the SQL column/bind names that `_columns_to_values` later looks payload references up by. The concrete `dict` test matches what SQLAlchemy actually hands: on the pinned 2.0.45 every parameter mapping in play subclasses `dict`, `immutabledict` included (`isinstance(immutabledict({'a': 1}), dict)` is True), so this arm fires for them and the comprehension rebuilds each one as a plain `dict`. That rebuild is what GUARANTEES the invariant `_columns_to_values` at line 841 then relies on when it tests `dict` alone — the two sites are a producer/consumer pair, not an inconsistency, and 841's narrowness is only honest for as long as this arm keeps materialising a plain `dict`. A Mapping that did NOT subclass `dict` would miss this arm and fall through to the leaf fallback unconverted, reaching `_columns_to_values` as a non-mapping and taking its `zip(..., strict=True)` arm, which raises rather than silently mis-binding — so the narrow test fails closed rather than fabricating. The arm masks nothing else either: keys are not filtered, and the total leaf fallback carries unrecognised types to `json.dumps`, which raises. INVALIDATED IF: this arm stops materialising a plain `dict` (the `_columns_to_values` invariant breaks and that site must widen in the same change); or a parameter mapping that is not a `dict` subclass enters the pipeline, at which point BOTH this arm and 841 should widen to `Mapping` together rather than one of them drifting.

journal.py:756 `if isinstance(parameters, Mapping):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance against an abstract base class. This site reads the RAW parameters SQLAlchemy passes to the execution hook, before `_normalize_parameters` has touched them, and that is why it tests the `Mapping` ABC rather than `dict`: the concrete container here is the dialect's and the driver's choice, not ELSPETH's, so the honest test is the contract-level one — 'this exposes keys I can iterate' — rather than a bet on a concrete class. Measured on the pinned SQLAlchemy 2.0.45, that breadth is not currently load-bearing: the parameter containers in play, `immutabledict` included, all subclass `dict` (`isinstance(immutabledict({'a': 1}), dict)` is True), so a `dict` test would match the same values today. `Mapping` is chosen because it stays correct without that coincidence holding. The mirror-image site at line 841 tests `dict` and is the reverse case — it runs AFTER normalisation over a value ELSPETH itself constructed, so the exact type is known and the narrow test is the honest one there. The two are deliberately different tests over the same conceptual value at two different points in the pipeline, and neither should be rewritten to match the other. The narrowing is a last-resort ordering rather than a guess: the function prefers `compiled.positiontup` (the authoritative compiled column order), falls back to the mapping's keys only when `positiontup` is empty, and falls back again to `compiled.params`. Iterating a `Mapping` yields its keys, which are the bind-parameter names this function must return. It is also not doing defensive Tier-3 parsing — the genuinely untrusted structural probe in this same function is the `.table` access guarded by `except AttributeError` at line 749, which is separately allowlisted; by the time control reaches line 756 the statement has already been confirmed to target the `calls` table. INVALIDATED IF: `parameters` starts arriving pre-normalised (the `Mapping` breadth would then be unmotivated and should narrow to `dict` to match 841); or the `positiontup` preference is removed, which would promote this fallback to the primary column-order source and demand a stronger check than 'is it a mapping'.

journal.py:841 `if isinstance(params, dict):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance selecting between two lookup strategies. This discriminates named from positional DBAPI parameter binding for payload-reference extraction: a dict is keyed by bind name so the columns are looked up by name, while a positional set must be zipped against the compiled column order. The `dict` test is correct HERE, as opposed to the `Mapping` test at line 756, because `params` reaches this function only via `record['parameters']` (or one element of it, at line 769), which `_normalize_parameters` has already rebuilt — line 730 materialises every mapping as a plain `dict` and lines 726/728 materialise every sequence as a `list`. That producer/consumer invariant was checked rather than assumed: line 730's arm is a concrete `dict` test, and every SQLAlchemy parameter mapping on the pinned 2.0.45 subclasses `dict` (`immutabledict` included), so each one does reach the rebuild. This site is therefore typing a value ELSPETH itself constructed one step earlier, which is the ADR-032 nominal-typing case rather than a hopeful structural check on third-party data. Both arms are fail-closed rather than defensive, which is what keeps this from being bug-hiding: the named arm does `params[col]`, raising `KeyError` if a declared payload column is absent, and the positional arm passes `strict=True` to `zip`, raising `ValueError` on any length mismatch between the compiled columns and the parameter set. A wrong or truncated mapping therefore crashes rather than silently producing a record with a missing `request_ref`/`response_ref`. INVALIDATED IF: `_normalize_parameters` stops guaranteeing a plain `dict` (widen this to `Mapping` in the same change), a caller starts passing raw pre-normalisation SQLAlchemy parameters, or either arm's fail-closed behaviour is softened — dropping `strict=True`, or replacing `params[col]` with `.get()`, would turn this dispatch into exactly the masking R5 exists to catch.
core/operations.py:R5:track_operation:as: operations.py:209 `if isinstance(db_error, contract_errors.TIER_1_ERRORS):`. FLAGGED PATTERN: isinstance classifying a caught exception. This is the crash-versus-propagate decision for an audit-write failure, and the classification is the whole point rather than a guard bolted on: `track_operation`'s `finally` block calls `recorder.complete_operation(...)`, and if that raises, the run has a completed operation with no audit record — a Tier-1 integrity violation. The rule is that a Tier-1 error (corruption, framework bug, invariant violation) propagates UNCONDITIONALLY as `raise db_error from original_exception`, overriding any in-flight operation-level exception, because audit corruption is categorically worse than any failure the operation itself hit; anything else defers to `original_exception` and propagates only when the operation had actually succeeded. The isinstance is not a substitute for a narrower `except` clause and must not be rewritten into one: the `logger.critical` audit-trail-incomplete record above it has to be emitted identically for BOTH classes, so splitting into `except contract_errors.TIER_1_ERRORS` / `except Exception` would duplicate that logging block and create two places for it to drift — a worse structure adopted only to move a lint finding. `TIER_1_ERRORS` is a tuple of exception classes ELSPETH defines in its own contracts module, so this is nominal typing over an owned taxonomy, and no arm is silent: every path either re-raises `db_error`, re-raises the original, or lets the original propagate, and all of them have already logged. INVALIDATED IF: `TIER_1_ERRORS` starts including third-party exception classes ELSPETH does not define (the tuple would stop being an owned taxonomy); the `logger.critical` call moves out of the shared path, since 'both classes need the same log' is the reason this is a classification rather than two except clauses; or any arm stops re-raising and starts swallowing the audit failure.
